title: Gastric Hypomotility Unmasking a Phytobezoar After Cryoballoon Pulmonary Vein Isolation

paragraphs.en: Epigastric or chest pain in the first hours after left atrial ablation is a diagnostic trap: it can equally signal a lethal vascular or esophageal complication or a benign, self‐limiting one. Gastric hypomotility from periesophageal vagal injury is an established, if uncommon, extracardiac effect of ablation [1, 2]; its association with a gastric phytobezoar is unusual. We describe a patient in whom cryoballoon pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) was followed by two sequential diagnostic pivots—marked gastric dilatation and then a phytobezoar.

A 62‐year‐old woman (body mass index 26.9 kg/m2) with EHRA class II atrial fibrillation refractory to propafenone underwent cryoballoon PVI. She had no diabetes, prior gastric or bariatric surgery, autonomic neuropathy, or psychiatric illness. She had received a proton pump inhibitor in 2021–2023 and again after rivaroxaban was started. Two upper gastrointestinal endoscopies in 2021 showed antral gastritis without a bezoar; no interval abdominal cross‐sectional imaging or repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was available before ablation. Pulmonary vein isolation was achieved and sinus rhythm restored (82 bpm); nadir balloon temperatures were −45°C and −49°C (240 s each) for the left‐sided pulmonary veins and −40°C and −43°C (180 s each) for the right‐sided veins. Luminal esophageal temperature was monitored throughout and stayed within the routine safety range, without triggering cryoenergy interruption. She was discharged asymptomatic.

Twenty‐four hours later she returned with epigastric pain. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm at 62 bpm without an ischemic pattern, and transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% with no pericardial effusion or other major abnormality. The immediate task was to exclude the emergencies that share this presentation after left atrial ablation: atrioesophageal fistula, esophageal perforation, mesenteric ischemia, and an acute coronary syndrome mimic. Comparison of the pre‐ablation and presentation chest radiographs already showed an interval increase in the gastric air–fluid level and distension (Figure 1).

Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography was the first pivot, converting a suspected catastrophe into a working diagnosis. It showed no evidence of mesenteric ischemia, esophageal perforation, or another acute vascular or esophageal complication, while revealing marked gastric dilatation consistent with acute gastric hypomotility (Figure 2A). No mechanical gastric outlet obstruction or extrinsic vascular compression was identified. Beyond the distension, the gastric lumen contained a well‐defined mass of heterogeneous material with entrapped gas—the mottled appearance characteristic of a bezoar [3] (Figure 2B)—which was nonetheless attributed at the time to food retained by the failing stomach.

A prokinetic agent (metoclopramide) was started, but symptoms persisted over the following week. Because symptoms remained unresolved, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed to evaluate for an intraluminal or mechanical cause. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy provided the second pivot, revealing a large phytobezoar with green vegetable‐fiber content and no pyloric stenosis, mucosal ulceration, or mechanical obstruction (Figure 3).

Management followed from the mechanism rather than from the size of the bezoar. A low‐fiber diet reduced ongoing substrate, and chemical dissolution with carbonated beverages, supplemented by nasogastric soda lavage, dissolved the agglomerate without endoscopic fragmentation or surgery [4]. Symptoms resolved within two weeks; endoscopy repeated at that point confirmed regression of the bezoar with a patent, uninjured pylorus (Figure 4). She remained asymptomatic at six months of follow‐up.

Periesophageal vagal branches governing gastric and pyloric function lie millimeters from the ablation target, and cryoballoon technology reduces but does not abolish this proximity. In this patient the left‐sided veins—nearest the esophagus—received the coldest and longest applications, a pattern that fits periesophageal neural involvement without proving it. That luminal esophageal temperature remained within the safety range does not argue against this mechanism: luminal thermometry samples the esophageal lumen rather than the vagal fibers coursing on its anterior surface, and periesophageal vagal injury is described despite unremarkable luminal readings [2]. That such injury underlies post‐ablation gastric hypomotility is established [1, 2], and symptomatic hypomotility after cryoballoon ablation is reported [5]. We claim no new mechanism.

When the bezoar formed cannot be determined. It was already visible on computed tomography 24 h after ablation, which argues against de novo formation in that interval. Gastritis and reduced gastric acidity are recognized predisposing factors [3]; antral gastritis on the 2021 endoscopies, together with long‐term acid suppression, makes a pre‐existing subclinical bezoar plausible. Post‐ablation hypomotility may have unmasked such a bezoar, but whether it contributed to bezoar growth cannot be established.

The most transferable lesson is one we learned late. The mottled intragastric mass with entrapped gas on the admission computed tomography—confirmed on radiological review as the characteristic appearance of a bezoar [3]—was present a full week before endoscopy, yet was read as food retained by a stomach already known to be emptying poorly. That interpretation is intuitive precisely because gastric stasis is expected in this setting, and this may explain why such a finding can be overlooked: the diagnosis hides behind the complication that brought it to light. In a patient with post‐ablation gastric dilatation, intragastric material with this appearance should therefore not be dismissed as an expected consequence of stasis, particularly when predisposing factors such as gastritis or long‐term acid suppression are present. Persistent or non‐improving symptoms despite initial conservative therapy should prompt focused review of the original imaging rather than continued escalation of prokinetics, moving endoscopy from a late exclusionary step to an early targeted one.

Limitations remain. Gastric emptying was not quantified objectively; the bezoar was recognized on the initial imaging only in retrospect, so we cannot claim that prospective recognition would have altered the outcome; and peri‐procedural sedation and analgesia may have transiently slowed emptying. A single case cannot identify patient‐level predictors or define a subgroup at increased risk of symptomatic phytobezoar after ablation. The link between ablation and the clinical presentation is therefore temporal and biologically plausible; a causal role in bezoar formation is not established. Early abdominal symptoms after ablation still require exclusion of catastrophic vascular and esophageal complications first; what this case adds thereafter is that the imaging obtained for that exclusion may already contain the answer.

figures.caption: Chest radiographs before (A) and 24 h after (B) cryoballoon ablation, showing an interval increase in the gastric air–fluid level and distension.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (coronal). (A) Marked gastric dilatation, with the magnified region indicated. (B) Magnified view of the gastric lumen showing a mottled intragastric mass with entrapped gas (dashed outline and arrows)—the characteristic appearance of a bezoar—present one week before endoscopy and attributed at the time to retained food.

figures.label: FIGURE 3
figures.caption: Initial upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (A, B): Large phytobezoar with vegetable‐fiber content (arrows); no pyloric stenosis, mucosal injury, or obstruction.

figures.label: FIGURE 4
figures.caption: Follow‐up endoscopy after dissolution therapy: (A) patent pylorus; (B) cardia and fundus clear; (C) former bezoar site with minimal residual food content (arrow).
